title: The last ridge
hookLine: Yudhishthira reaches the top with only a dog beside him, and won't enter heaven without it
tomorrow: why would a Zen teacher picture a man hunting for an ox?

lines: ONLY ONE IS STILL BESIDE HIM.
cards: Somewhere in a drawer or a notes app there's the first thing you wrote when you started something. This path began with one breath at the bottom of the hill.
Near the end of the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi give up their kingdom and set out on foot for the mountains. A dog follows them.
On the climb, one by one, the others fall and are left behind. Yudhishthira, the eldest, keeps walking. By the end of the climb, only one companion is still beside him.

teach.b: The dog. And then the god Indra arrives in a chariot to carry Yudhishthira into heaven. Get in, he says, but the dog stays here.
Yudhishthira refuses. To abandon one who is devoted to you, he says, is a grave wrong, and he won't do it, not even for heaven. Then the dog changes shape.

It's Dharma, the god of righteousness, who has been testing him. That's the Mahabharata's teaching at the summit: dharma, being true to what's right, kept to the very end, even toward the smallest one who walked with you.
So the question on a last ridge isn't how far did I climb. It's who and what did I stay true to on the way. Another voice, from the Christian Bible.

teach.h: PAUL: I HAVE KEPT THE FAITH.
teach.b: Near the end of his life, Paul writes to Timothy: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." The shared thing: at the end, what counts is faithfulness kept.
And the honest difference: Paul's faith is in Christ, and he looks for a crown from the Lord. Yudhishthira's test is dharma, shown to a dog at heaven's gate.
Two traditions, each counting faithfulness at the finish, each in its own way.

how: Hindus retell the Pandavas' last journey from the Mahabharata, with Yudhishthira's refusal to abandon the dog, as a picture of dharma kept to the end; people who borrow it look back at where they started and who walked with them.

o: the last stretch, where you see what you stayed true to
the hardest climb a person will ever face
the point where you finally stop and turn back

games.q: the last climb: tap the pairs.
p: came in a chariot: leave the dog

s: Yudhishthira got into heaven by leaving everything behind, even the dog
the opposite. he refused to go without the dog, and the dog was Dharma testing him.
Paul and the Mahabharata both count faithfulness at the end
a shared thing, said differently: Paul's faith in Christ, Yudhishthira's dharma toward a dog.

games.q: your friend finishes a long degree and says, 'i didn't end up where i planned.' what fits the last ridge?
o: ask who and what she stayed true to on the way; that's what the top tests.
point out how far she got; distance is the real measure of a journey.
tell her plans don't matter, since nobody ends up where they meant to.
games.why: Indra told Yudhishthira to leave the dog. he refused, and the dog was Dharma. the test at the top was faithfulness.

practice: If you kept a first note from when you started this path, find it and read it slowly, once. If you didn't, remember in one sentence what you hoped for at the start.
Then sit with it, and with whoever has walked beside you since, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The last ridge: the final stretch before the top, where the Mahabharata asks not how far you came, but what you stayed true to.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dharma, what is right and true; in this story also the god who takes the dog's shape.

carryVoice: Carry this: the last ridge, where Yudhishthira wouldn't leave the one who walked with him. Onward.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva (the Pandavas' last journey; the falls on the climb; Indra and the dog; the dog revealed as Dharma)
